Extending the Trace of a Pivotal Monoidal Functor
Leonard Hardiman

Abstract
. We consider a pivotal monoidal functor whose domain is a modular tensor category (MTC). We show that the trace of such a functor naturally extends to a representation of the corresponding tube category. As irreducible representations of the tube category are indexed by pairs of simple objects in the underlying MTC, the simple multiplicities of this representation form a candidate modular invariant matrix. In general, this matrix will not be modular invariant, however it will always commute with the T-matrix. Furthermore, under certain additional conditions on the original functor, it is shown that the corresponding representation of the tube category is a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra. Such algebras are known to be connected to modular invariants, in particular a result of Kong and Runkel implies that the matrix of simple multiplicities commutes with the S-matrix if and only if the dimension of the algebra is equal to the dimension of the underlying MTC. Finally, we apply these techniques to certain pivotal monoidal functors arising from module categories over the Temperley-Lieb category and the associated MTC. This provides a novel explanation of the A-D-E pattern appearing in the classification of A 1 ( 1 ) A_{1}^{(1)} modular invariants.



1.
Introduction

The principal aim of this article is to describe a procedure which associates an integer non-negative matrix to a pivotal monoidal functor
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
. This procedure is motived by the particular case when
\mathcal{C}
is the category of modules over a vertex operator algebra and
\mathcal{M}
is a module category over
\mathcal{C}
. In this case
\mathcal{M}
may be thought of as describing a boundary conformal field theory and the resulting matrix as the modular invariant of the corresponding closed conformal field theory. This introduction therefore provides a brief review of the relevant mathematical physics followed by a more detailed description of the contents of this paper.

An important property of a (closed) conformal field theory (CFT) is that it has two chiral halves: a holomorphic (or “left-moving”) half and an anti-holomorphic (or “right-moving”) half. In other words, the state space
H
of the theory decomposes into the direct sum

\displaystyle H=\bigoplus\limits_{IJ}Z_{IJ}\ H_{I}\otimes\overline{H}_{J}

(1)

where the
Z_{IJ}
are multiplicity spaces and the
H_{I}
range over the irreducible modules of a vertex operator algebra (VOA)
\mathcal{V}
(we assume that our CFT is non-heterotic, i.e. that
H_{I}
and
H_{J}
are modules over the same VOA). The physical “uniqueness of the vacuum” assumption imposes that
Z_{\tid,\tid}=\mathbb{C}
where
\tid
is such that
H_{\tid}=\mathcal{V}
. The CFT is called
rational
if
\mathcal{V}
admits only finitely many irreducible modules; we assume that this is the case from now on. The decomposition of
H
given by (
1
) implies that

\displaystyle Z(\tau)=\sum\limits_{IJ}\dim Z_{IJ}\ \chi_{I}(\tau)\chi_{J}(\tau)^{*}

(2)

where
Z
is the
partition function
of the theory, i.e.
Z(\tau)
is the value of the theory on the torus corresponding to
\tau\in\mathbb{H}
and
\chi_{I}
is the character of the irreducible VOA module
H_{I}
. As conformal structures on the torus are parametrized by
\mathbb{H}/\PSL_{2}(\mathbb{Z})
, we require that
Z
be invariant under the action of
\PSL_{2}(\mathbb{Z})
on
\mathbb{H}
.

The category of modules over a VOA has an extremely rich structure: it forms a
modular tensor category
(MTC)
[
Hua05
]
. MTCs possess many nice properties (they are semisimple, rigid, braided…) and in particular they come equipped with a representation of
\PSL_{2}(\mathbb{Z})
given by their
modular data
. Let
\mathcal{I}
be (an indexing set for) a complete set of irreducible objects in an MTC. The modular data is composed of two
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrices known as the S-matrix and the T-matrix; they are denoted by
\mathcal{S}
and
\mathcal{T}
respectively. Using the graphical calculus of MTCs, the entries of these matrices are given as follows,

The condition that the partition function of a CFT is invariant under the action of
\PSL_{2}(\mathbb{Z})
on
\mathbb{H}
may be rephrased as requiring that the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix with entries
\dim Z_{IJ}
commutes with the modular data of the category of modules over the relevant VOA. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 1.1
.

For a modular tensor category with tensor identity
\tid
and complete set of simples
\mathcal{I}
, a
modular invariant
is a non-negative integer
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix that commutes with the modular data and whose
(\tid,\tid)
-entry is
1
.

A popular strategy when attempting to classify CFTs is to fix a VOA
\mathcal{V}
and search for all compatible partition functions. From the above discussion we see that this is related to finding the modular invariants associated to the MTC of modules over
\mathcal{V}
. An example in which this has been successfully carried out is provided by the VOA constructed from the affine Lie algebra
A_{1}^{(1)}
together with a positive integer
k
, via the Sugawara construction
[
Sug68
]
. The category of modules in this case is the category of integrable highest weight modules of
A_{1}^{(1)}
at level
k
, denoted
\Rep_{k}A_{1}^{(1)}
. In 1986 Cappelli, Itzykson and Zuber classified all possible modular invariants in this context and, to their surprise, the classification followed an A-D-E pattern
[
CIZ87
]
. The appearance of this pattern intrigued many researchers in the field and was the subject of much speculation
[
Gan00
,
Zub02
,
KO02
]
. The first explanation of the pattern was provided by an operator algebra technique known as
\alpha
-induction
, due to Böckenhauer and Evans
[
BE98
]
. This technique relates the A-D-E classification of Goodman-de la Harpe-Jones subfactors to Cappelli, Itzykson and Zuber’s classification
[
BE01
,
Ocn99
]
.

When translating from the operator algebra language to the purely categorical one an inclusion of subfactors corresponds to a module category. Modules categories also have a physical interpretation. In 1989 Cardy showed that the algebraic data of an
annular partition function
in a
boundary
CFT (as opposed to the toroidal partition function
Z
) is given by a module category over the corresponding MTC
[
Car89
]
. From a physical point of view the correspondence between module categories and modular invariants should therefore be thought of as a “closing up” just as an annulus closes up into a torus. Mathematically we would expect this “closing up” to correspond to taking the
trace
, in some suitable sense, of the module category. A notion of trace does exist for module categories (and more generally for monoidal functors), however it simply produces a representation of the MTC. A priori it is not at all clear how to associate a non-negative integer
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix to this representation. This article presents a solution to this problem by extending the representation to take values on the
tube category
of the underlying MTC.

For a spherical fusion category
\mathcal{C}
, the tube category, denoted
\mathcal{TC}
, shares the same objects as
\mathcal{C}
but has more morphisms i.e.
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\leq\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,Y)
. The intuition is that whereas morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
may be represented graphically as diagrams drawn on a bounded region of the plane, morphisms in
\mathcal{TC}
are given by diagrams drawn on a cylinder. Section
3
describes how, for
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
a pivotal monoidal functor, the trace of
\mathcal{M}
naturally extends to a representation of
\mathcal{TC}
, which we denote
\mathcal{TM}
. This extension may also be understood from the perspective of work done by Bruguieres and Natale
[
BN11
,
BN14
]
; this is explained in greater detail in Remark
6.8
. As irreducible representations of the tube category are indexed by pairs of elements in
\mathcal{I}
, decomposing
\mathcal{TM}
into irreducibles gives a non-negative integer
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix,
Z(\mathcal{TM})
. For
F
a representation of
\mathcal{TC}
,
F
is called T-invariant (respectively S-invariant) if
Z(F)
commutes with
\mathcal{T}
(respectively
\mathcal{S}
).

Section
4
gives a graphical characterisation of T-invariance when
\mathcal{C}
is an MTC. In particular, Theorem
4.4
proves that
F
is T-invariant if and only if
F(t_{X})=\id_{F(X)}
where
t_{X}\in\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(X)
is the
twist morphism
on
X
, see (
4
). An immediate corollary of this is that
\mathcal{TM}
is T-invariant; this corollary will later be strengthened to Theorem
7.5
which only assumes that
\mathcal{C}
is pre-modular. Section
5
starts by showing that, in general,
Z(\mathcal{TM})
fails to be S-invariant. Indeed, when
\mathcal{M}
is the identity functor on
\mathcal{C}
,
Z(\mathcal{TM})
is given by

\displaystyle Z(\mathcal{TM})_{IJ}=\begin{cases}1\quad\text{if $I=J=\tid$}\\
0\quad\text{else}\end{cases}

which doesn’t commute with the S-matrix in general (this will be explained in greater detail in Example
5.2
). However, under the assumption that
\mathcal{M}
is indecomposable and takes value in a category whose idempotent completion is multifusion, Theorem
6.7
proves that
\mathcal{TM}
is a haploid, symmetric, commutative, Frobenius algebra. By a
result of Kong and Runkel

[
KR09
, Theorem 3.4]
this implies that
Z(\mathcal{TM})
commutes with the S-matrix if and only if the dimension of
\mathcal{TM}
is equal to the dimension of
\mathcal{C}
. This condition on the dimension of
\mathcal{TM}
is equivalent to requiring that

(\mathcal{S}\ Z(\mathcal{TM})\ \mathcal{S}^{-1})_{\tid,\tid}=Z(\mathcal{TM})_{\tid,\tid}

and is therefore always a necessary condition for S-invariance.

Section
7
describes a categorical formulation of
\alpha
-induction given by Ostrik
[
Ost03
, Section 5]
. Let
\mathcal{C}
be a pre-modular tensor category and let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\End(\mathcal{B})
be a module category. Following
[
Ost03
]
, we define a subspace
\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(I,J^{\vee})<\Hom_{\End(\mathcal{B})}(\mathcal{M}(I),\mathcal{M}(J^{\vee}))
defined by the condition that
\beta\in\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(I,J^{\vee})
satisfies, for all
X
in
\mathcal{C}
,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(I)\otimes\mathcal{M}(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(X)\otimes\mathcal{M}(I)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(J^{\vee})\otimes\mathcal{M}(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(X)\otimes\mathcal{M}(J^{\vee})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta\otimes\id}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(\overline{\sigma}_{XI})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\otimes\beta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(\sigma_{XJ^{\vee}})}
\circlearrowleft

where
\sigma
and
\overline{\sigma}
are the braiding on
\mathcal{C}
and its opposite respectively. Ostrik’s categorical formulation of
\alpha
-induction states that, when the dimension of all the objects in
\mathcal{C}
are positive, the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix with entries given by the dimension of
\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(I,J^{\vee})
is a modular invariant. Theorem
7.4
proves that, when
\mathcal{M}

induces a pivotal structure on its image
, the
\mathcal{TM}
construction may be applied and
Z(\mathcal{TM})
will produce the same matrix as
\alpha
-induction. Furthermore, this application of the
\mathcal{TM}
construction to module categories leads us to Corollary
7.6
which states that, when
\mathcal{M}
is an indecomposable module category that induces a pivotal structure on its full image,
\mathcal{TM}
is a haploid, symmetric, commutative, Frobenius algebra.

Finally, Section
8
applies the
\mathcal{TM}
construction to a class of examples arising from module categories over the Temperley-Lieb category. The Temperley-Lieb category may be thought of as a diagrammatic presentation of the previously discussed category
\Rep_{k}A_{1}^{(1)}
. It is shown that all module categories over
\Rep_{k}A_{1}^{(1)}
induce a pivotal structure on their full image and so the
\mathcal{TM}
construction may be applied. This leads to a new explanation of the A-D-E pattern that appears in the Cappelli-Itzykson-Zuber classification of
A_{1}^{(1)}
modular invariants.

There are pre-existing methods for relating module categories to modular invariant
2
2

2

As defined in
[
Kon08
, Section 6]
, cf. Remark
5.5
.
Frobenius algebras in
\CC
. Any module category over
\mathcal{C}
may be realised (non-uniquely) as the category of modules of an algebra in
\mathcal{C}

[
Ost03
]
. The
full centre construction

[
FFRS08
, Definition 4.9]
then associates a modular invariant, commutative, symmetric Frobenius algebra in
\CC
to a special (as defined in, for example,
[
KR09
]
), symmetric Frobenius algebra in
\mathcal{C}

[
KR09
, Theorem 3.18]
. Furthermore every modular invariant, commutative, symmetric Frobenius algebra in
\CC
may be realised in this way
[
KR09
, Theorem 3.22]
.

The full centre construction may also be described in terms of the module category directly
[
DKR15
, Section 3.1]
. Schaumann has worked on characterising the condition that the module category be equivalent to the category of modules of a special symmetric Frobenius algebra purely in terms of the module category itself. In particular he has shown that it is equivalent to requiring that the module category admits a
module trace

[
Sch13
]
. It is possible that this could be related to the condition identified in this article: that the module category induce a pivotal structure on its full image.

Conventions.
For
V
and
W
vector spaces, we write “
V=W
” to indicate that
V
and
W
are isomorphic under an isomorphism that should be clear from the context. Unless otherwise specified, a sum over a variable object ranges over a complete set of simple objects. Similarly, unless otherwise specified, a sum over a variable morphism ranges over a basis of the appropriate
\Hom
-space. All categories are assumed to be enriched over the category of finite dimensional vector spaces. For a category
\mathcal{C}
we use
\mathcal{RC}
to denote the category of
contravariant
functors from
\mathcal{C}
to the category of finite dimensional vector spaces. An object in
\mathcal{RC}
is called a
representation
of
\mathcal{C}
. For an object
X
in a pivotal category we use
X^{\vee}
to denote a dual object to
X
. The corresponding annihilation and creation maps are then denoted
\ann_{X}
and
\cre_{X}
respectively. Much of the work carried out in this article will be done relative to a fixed spherical fusion category
\mathcal{C}
, when taking tensor products in this category we will omit the “
\otimes
” symbol and write
XY
for
X\otimes Y
. However, we will write the “
\otimes
” symbol when taking a tensor product in any other category. Many of the arguments in this article exploit the graphical calculus of spherical fusion categories. For an exposition of these techniques see, for example,
[
Har20
]
. In particular, the unit and associativity isomorphisms are suppressed as well as the pivotal structure. All diagrams are read top to bottom.

2.
Preliminaries on the Tube Category

We start by recording some results on the tube category, which will be used throughout; for more details on these results see
[
HK19
]
and
[
Har20
]
. Let
\fld
be an algebraically closed field and let
\mathcal{C}
be a spherical fusion category over
\fld
with complete set of simples
\mathcal{I}
. The
tube category
of
\mathcal{C}
, denoted
\mathcal{TC}
, is a category whose objects coincide with those of
\mathcal{C}
and whose
\Hom
-spaces are given by

\displaystyle\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,Y)\vcentcolon=\bigoplus\limits_{S}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(SX,YS)

where, as per our conventions, the direct sum ranges over
\mathcal{I}
and the monoidal product symbol is suppressed. To depict a morphism in
\mathcal{TC}
using the graphical calculus of spherical fusion categories we take
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(GX,YG)
and write

This intuition, together with the associativity of the tensor product, guarantee that composition in
\mathcal{TC}
is associative.

Remark 2.1
.

We note that the tensor product is merely weakly associative and yet composition in a category must be strongly associative. However, this is not an issue as the associator isomorphisms will simply modify the basis appearing in (
2
) leaving the composition unchanged.

Remark 2.2
.

If we consider the algebra
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}\left(\bigoplus_{S}S\right)
we recover Ocneanu’s
tube algebra

[
Ocn94
]
. As
\bigoplus_{S}S
is a projective generator in
\mathcal{TC}
, the tube algebra is Morita equivalent to
\mathcal{TC}
, i.e. its category of representations is equivalent to
\mathcal{RTC}
.

Remark 2.3
.

Let
\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{C})
denote the Grothendieck ring of
\mathcal{C}
and let
\mathcal{K}_{\fld}(\mathcal{C})
denote
\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{C})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\fld
. Then
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid)
and
\mathcal{K}_{\fld}(\mathcal{C})
are canonically isomorphic algebras. Indeed,
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid)=\bigoplus_{S}\End(S)=\bigoplus_{S}\fld
is precisely the underlying vector space of
\mathcal{K}_{\fld}(\mathcal{C})
. Furthermore, composition in
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid)
corresponds to the tensor product in
\mathcal{K}_{\fld}(\mathcal{C})
.

Remark 2.4
.

The canonical inclusion
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)\hookrightarrow\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,Y)
realises
\mathcal{C}
as a wide subcategory of
\mathcal{TC}
.

Remark
2.4
suggests the following natural question: for a given representation of
\mathcal{C}
(i.e. an object in
\mathcal{RC}
) what additional data could be provided to specify a unique extension to an object
F
in
\mathcal{RTC}
? This question is answered in
[
Har20
]
by considering the value of the extended functor on morphisms in
\mathcal{TC}
of the form

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{array}\quad\text{where $\alpha=\id_{GXG}$.}

Proposition 2.5
.

Let
F
be in
\mathcal{RC}
and let
\kappa_{G,X}\colon F(GX)\to F(XG)
be a collection of isomorphisms which are natural in
G
and
X
and satisfy
\kappa_{H,XG}\circ\kappa_{G,HX}=\kappa_{GH,X}
. Then there is a unique object
(F,\kappa)
in
\mathcal{RTC}
which satisfies
(F,\kappa)(X)=F(X)
for all
X
in
\mathcal{C}
,
(F,\kappa)(\alpha)=F(\alpha)
for all
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)
and
(F,\kappa)(\alpha_{G})=\kappa_{G,X}
where
\alpha=\id_{GXG}
for all
G,X
in
\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

See Proposition 6.1 in
[
Har20
]
. ∎

Remark 2.6
.

As
\mathcal{C}
is a fusion category the Yoneda embedding gives an equivalence between
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{RC}
. As described in Section 7 of
[
Har20
]
, the data required to extend the image of
X
under the Yoneda embedding to
\mathcal{TC}
(as given by Proposition
2.5
) corresponds to a half braiding on
X
. Combining these facts yields an equivalence between
Z(\mathcal{C})
and
\mathcal{RTC}
, where
Z(\mathcal{C})
is the
Drinfeld centre
of
\mathcal{C}
.

We now equip
\mathcal{C}
with a (balanced)
braiding
, in other words,
\mathcal{C}
is a
pre-modular tensor category
. Our main tool for studying
\mathcal{TC}

). As described at the start of

,
[
Har20
, Proposition 7.4]
implies that the canonical braided functor

satisfies

\displaystyle\Phi(X\boxtimes Y)=(XY,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})^{\sharp}\vcentcolon=\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(\Blank,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})

(8)

where
\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(Z,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})=\{\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(Z,XY)\mid\epsilon_{X}^{Y}\circ\alpha=\alpha\}
. Combining this with the fact that
\Phi
is an equivalence when
\mathcal{C}
is modular (see
[
EGNO15
, Proposition 8.20.12]
) and we obtain the result that, in the modular case, the set
\{\epsilon_{I}^{J}\}_{I,J\in\mathcal{I}}
forms a complete set of orthogonal primitive idempotents in
\mathcal{TC}
.

The isomorphism is in fact given by the embedding of the braiding on
\mathcal{C}
into
\mathcal{TC}
. Therefore the isomorphism class of
\epsilon_{X}^{Y}
is really determined by the fact that the
X
strand is
under
-braided and the
Y
strand is
over
-braided. This motivates the notation.

Remark 2.8
.

We recall from Remark
2.3
that
\mathcal{K}_{\fld}(\mathcal{C})=\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid)
. By Corollary 8.2 in
[
Har20
]
we have

\displaystyle\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid,\epsilon_{I}^{J})=\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(\tid,IJ)=\delta_{J,I^{\vee}}\fld\quad\forall I,J\in\mathcal{I}.

As
\{\epsilon_{I}^{J}\}_{I,J\in\mathcal{I}}
forms a complete set of primitive idempotents in
\mathcal{TC}
we may conclude that
\mathcal{K}_{\fld}(\mathcal{C})
is a commutative semisimple algebra generated by a set of primitive orthogonal idempotents indexed by
\mathcal{I}
.

Definition 3.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be spherical fusion category, let
\mathcal{D}
be a pivotal monoidal category and let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a pivotal monoidal functor. Then

\mathcal{TM}\colon\mathcal{TC}\to\Vect

\mathcal{RTC}
obtained by applying Proposition
2.5
to
\Tr\mathcal{M}
and
\kappa_{G,X}
as given by (
10

\mathcal{TM}

\displaystyle\mathcal{TM}(\alpha_{G})\colon\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M}(Y),\tid)

Remark 3.2
.

It is possible to define the
\mathcal{TM}
construction for functors
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
that are not pivotal by simply adding in the image of the pivotal structure in
\mathcal{C}
to (
10
). However, doing so would not be compatible with our graphical conventions: the pivotal structure in
\mathcal{C}
(which is suppressed from the graphical calculus) would be mapped to a morphism in
\mathcal{D}
which could fail to be the corresponding pivotal structure (and thus not be suppressed from the graphical calculus).

Remark 3.3
.

When
\mathcal{D}
is linear it is straightforward to check that

\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{M}_{2}\colon X\mapsto\mathcal{M}_{1}(X)\oplus\mathcal{M}_{2}(X)

satisfies
\mathcal{TM}=\mathcal{TM}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{TM}_{2}
.

We now once again suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is equipped with a (balanced) braiding and is therefore a pre-modular tensor category. For an object
F
in
\mathcal{RTC}
we consider the
\Hom
-space

\displaystyle F_{X}^{Y}\vcentcolon=\Hom_{\mathcal{RTC}}((XY,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})^{\sharp},F)=\{\alpha\in F(XY)\mid F(\epsilon_{X}^{Y})(\alpha)=\alpha\}.

Definition 3.6
.

For any
F
in
\mathcal{RTC}
one may consider the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
integer matrix.

\displaystyle Z(F)\vcentcolon=(\dim F_{I}^{J})_{I,J\in\mathcal{I}}.

Remark 3.7
.

We recall that, if
\mathcal{C}
is modular, the set
\{(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}\}_{I,J\in\mathcal{I}}
forms a complete set of simples in
\mathcal{RTC}
. Therefore an entry of
Z(F)
simply gives the multiplicity of the corresponding simple object in
F
.

4.
T-Invariance

Definition 4.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a pre-modular tensor category and let
\mathcal{T}
be the T-matrix of
\mathcal{C}
as defined by (
1
). We call an object
F
in
\mathcal{RTC}

T-invariant
if
Z(F)
commutes with
\mathcal{T}
.

\mathcal{C}

Lemma 4.2
.

For all
\beta\in\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,Y)
we have,

\displaystyle\beta\circ t_{X}=t_{Y}\circ\beta.

Proof.

Let
\beta
be in
\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,Y)
. As any morphism in
\mathcal{TC}
may be written as a linear combination of elements of the form
\alpha_{G}
we may assume w.l.o.g. that
\beta=\alpha_{G}
. We have

as desired. ∎

As described in Section
2
, if
\mathcal{C}
is modular then
\epsilon_{I}^{J}
is a primitive idempotent. In particular we have
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\epsilon_{I}^{J})=\fld
. However, by Lemma
4.2
, we have

\displaystyle\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}\circ\epsilon_{I}^{J}=\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}=\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}

so
\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}\in\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\epsilon_{I}^{J})
. Therefore
\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}=\lambda\epsilon_{I}^{J}
for some
\lambda\in\fld
. This turns out to also be true in the case when
\mathcal{C}
is only assumed to be a pre-modular tensor category.

Proposition 4.3
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a pre-modular tensor category and let
I,J
be in
\mathcal{I}
. Then

\displaystyle\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{II}}{\mathcal{T}_{JJ}}\epsilon_{I}^{J}.

We may now prove the main result of this section.

Theorem 4.4
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a modular tensor category and let
F
be an object in
\mathcal{RTC}
.
F
is T-invariant if and only if
F(t_{X})=\id_{F(X)}
for all
X
in
\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

As
\mathcal{C}
is modular the
(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}
form a complete set of simple objects in
\mathcal{TC}
. We can therefore decompose
F
as

\displaystyle F=\bigoplus\limits_{IJ}F_{I}^{J}\vprod(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}.

Evaluating this on
t_{X}
gives

\displaystyle F(t_{X})=\bigoplus\limits_{IJ}\id_{F_{I}^{J}}\otimes(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}(t_{X}).

By Lemma
4.2
and Proposition
4.3
we have, for
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,\epsilon_{I}^{J})
,

\displaystyle(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}(t_{X})(\alpha)=\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ\alpha\circ t_{X}=\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ t_{IJ}\circ\alpha=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{II}}{\mathcal{T}_{JJ}}\epsilon_{I}^{J}\circ\alpha=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{II}}{\mathcal{T}_{JJ}}\alpha.

Therefore

\displaystyle\bigoplus\limits_{IJ}\id_{F_{I}^{J}}\otimes(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}(t_{X})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus\limits_{IJ}\frac{\mathcal{T}_{II}}{\mathcal{T}_{JJ}}\id_{F_{I}^{J}\otimes(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}(X)}.

This is equal to
\id_{F(X)}
if and only if
F_{I}^{J}\neq 0
implies
\frac{\mathcal{T}_{II}}{\mathcal{T}_{JJ}}=1
. As
\mathcal{T}
is diagonal that is precisely the condition that
Z(F)
commutes with
\mathcal{T}
. ∎

5.
S-Invariance and Frobenius Algebras

Definition 5.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a pre-modular tensor category and let
\mathcal{S}
be the S-matrix of
\mathcal{C}
as defined by (
1
). We call an object
F
in
\mathcal{RTC}

S-invariant
if
Z(F)
commutes with
\mathcal{S}
.

We start with an example which illustrates that, even when
\mathcal{C}
is modular,
\mathcal{TM}
is
not
necessarily S-invariant.

for all
Z
in
\mathcal{C}
. Post-composing this equality with
\id_{Z}\otimes\ann_{J}
and taking the trace implies
\mathcal{S}_{ZJ}=d(Z)d(J)
for all
Z
in
\mathcal{C}
. Therefore the
J
-th column in
\mathcal{S}
is proportional to the
\tid
-th column. As
\mathcal{C}
is modular this implies
J=\tid
. In summary, we have

\displaystyle Z(\mathcal{TM})_{IJ}=\begin{cases}1\quad\text{if $I=J=\tid$}\\
0\quad\text{else}.\end{cases}

Conjugating this matrix with
\mathcal{S}
and using the fact that
\mathcal{S}_{I,J}=d(\mathcal{C})\mathcal{S}_{I,J^{\vee}}^{-1}
gives us

\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{S}\ Z(\mathcal{TM})\ \mathcal{S}^{-1}\right)_{\tid\tid}=\frac{1}{d(\mathcal{C})}

implying that
\mathcal{S}
-invariance will fail whenever
d(\mathcal{C})\neq 1
.

However, when
\mathcal{C}
is a modular tensor category, we have a helpful theorem from
[
KR09
]
. For the prerequisite definitions on Frobenius algebras see Definition
A.1
.

Theorem 5.3

(Theorem 3.4,
[
KR09
]
)
.

Let
A
be a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra in
\CC
. Then the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix with entries
\hom(I\boxtimes J,A)
commutes with the S-matrix of
\mathcal{C}
(where, as before,
\hom
denotes the dimension of the relevant
\Hom
-space) if and only if

\displaystyle d(A)=d(\mathcal{C}).

(14)

Remark 5.4
.

We note that

\displaystyle d(A)

\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{IJ}\hom_{\CC}(I\boxtimes J,A)d(I\boxtimes J)

\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{IJ}\hom_{\CC}(I\boxtimes J,A)d(I)d(J)

\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{IJ}\mathcal{S}_{\tid,I}\hom_{\CC}(I\boxtimes J,A)\mathcal{S}_{J,\tid}.

As
\mathcal{S}_{I,J}=d(\mathcal{C})\mathcal{S}_{I,J^{\vee}}^{-1}
, Condition (
14
) is precisely the condition that the matrix with entries
\hom(I\boxtimes J,A)
commutes with the S-matrix evaluated at
(\tid,\tid)
for an arbitrary object
A
in
\CC
. Condition (
14
) is therefore certainly necessary, the content of the theorem is that, when
A
is a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra, it is also sufficient.

Remark 5.5
.

[
KR09
, Theorem 3.4]
actually proves that when
A
is a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra (
14
) implies an equality which is strictly stronger than the result stated here. In particular,
[
KR09
, Theorem 3.4]
proves that
A
will be a
modular invariant algebra
. This notion is defined and motivated in
[
Kon08
, Section 6]
.

Remark 5.6
.

As explained in the proof of
[
KR09
, Theorem 3.4]
, there exists an MTC (the category of of local
A
-modules) whose dimension is given by
\frac{d(\mathcal{C})^{2}}{d(A)^{2}}
. Combining this with the fact that any MTC over the complex numbers has dimension at least 1
[
ENO05
, Theorem 2.3.]
tells us that, in the case when
\fld=\mathbb{C}
, the dimension of
A
cannot exceed
d(\mathcal{C})
.

We recall that, when
\mathcal{C}
is modular,
\Phi\colon\CC\to\mathcal{RTC}
is an equivalence and
I\boxtimes J\mapsto(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}
. Therefore, for
F
in
\mathcal{RTC}
, the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
matrix with entries
\hom_{\mathcal{RTC}}(\Phi(I\boxtimes J),F)
is precisely
Z(F)
. The goal of the following section is to prove that
\mathcal{TM}
is a commutative algebra in
\mathcal{RTC}
, and then, under a further condition on
\mathcal{M}
, to show that it is also a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra.

The above stated goal assumes that
\mathcal{RTC}
is a braided pivotal monoidal category; this is indeed the case as
\mathcal{RTC}=Z(\mathcal{C})
(see Remark
2.6
) and
Z(\mathcal{C})
admits a canonical MTC structure
[
EGNO15
, Corollary 8.20.13]
. To achieve this goal we are therefore going to have to work with the monoidal product, braiding and pivotal structure that
\mathcal{RTC}
inherits from
Z(\mathcal{C})
. In general this is not easy; for instance it is hard to express the tensor product of two generic objects in
\mathcal{RTC}
. However, if we restrict our attention to functors coming from idempotents of the form (
2
) these structures may be described graphically.

We note that this product does not give a monoidal product as there is no unit. The tensor identity
\tid
in
\mathcal{C}
fails to give a unit as the functor

\displaystyle\Blank\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\tid\colon\mathcal{TC}\to\mathcal{TC}

maps
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(X,Y)
to
d(\mathcal{C})\alpha_{\tid}\in\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)
and so the unit isomorphisms fail to be natural.

Remark 5.8
.

The scalars appearing in (
5.7
) are chosen to guarantee that
\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}
is well-behaved with respect to idempotents of the form
\epsilon_{X}^{Y}
. Indeed, we have

\displaystyle(XYAB,\epsilon_{X}^{Y}\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}=(XAYB,\epsilon_{XA}^{YB})^{\sharp}

where the isomorphism is once again given by the braiding.

Proposition 5.9
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a modular tensor category. For
X,Y
objects in
\mathcal{C}
, we have

\displaystyle(XY,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})^{\sharp}\otimes(AB,\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}=(XAYB,\epsilon_{XA}^{YB})^{\sharp}=(XYAB,\epsilon_{X}^{Y}\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}.

Furthermore, for
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(\epsilon_{X}^{Y},\epsilon_{A}^{B})
and
\beta\in\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(\epsilon_{X^{\prime}}^{Y^{\prime}},\epsilon_{A^{\prime}}^{B^{\prime}})
, we have

\displaystyle\alpha\otimes\beta=\alpha\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\beta

where
\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}
is the associative product given by Definition
5.7
.

Proof.

By (
8
), we have

\displaystyle(XY,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})^{\sharp}\otimes(AB,\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}

\displaystyle=\Phi(X\boxtimes Y)\otimes\Phi(A\boxtimes B)

\displaystyle=\Phi(XA\boxtimes YB)

\displaystyle=(XAYB,\epsilon_{XA}^{YB})^{\sharp}

where
\Phi
is as defined in Section
2
. As described in Remark
5.8
, we then have

\displaystyle(XAYB,\epsilon_{XA}^{YB})^{\sharp}=(XYAB,\epsilon_{X}^{Y}\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}.

where the natural isomorphism is given by the braiding. This proves the first half of the proposition.

Let
f,f^{\prime},g,g^{\prime}
be in
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,A)
,
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\prime},A^{\prime})
,
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(Y,B)
and
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(Y^{\prime},B^{\prime})
respectively and let
\alpha
and
\beta
be given by

\displaystyle\alpha=\Phi(f\boxtimes g)\quad\text{and}\quad\beta=\Phi(f^{\prime}\boxtimes g^{\prime}).

(16)

Then

\displaystyle\alpha\otimes\beta

\displaystyle=\Phi((f\boxtimes g)\otimes(f\boxtimes g))

\displaystyle=\Phi((f\otimes f^{\prime})\boxtimes(g\otimes g^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=\alpha\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\beta.

as desired.

As
\Phi
is fully faithful any morphism in
\mathcal{TC}
may be written as a sum of morphisms of the form (
16
). This implies
\alpha\otimes\beta=\alpha\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\beta
for arbitrary
\alpha
and
\beta
. ∎

(AB,\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}

respectively. Note the tensor identity in
\mathcal{RTC}
is
(\tid,\epsilon_{\tid}^{\tid})^{\sharp}
and
not

\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(\Blank,\tid)
.

As
\mathcal{TM}
is not of the form
(XY,\epsilon_{X}^{Y})^{\sharp}
equipping it with the structure of a Frobenius algebra directly is difficult. However, as we are assuming that
\mathcal{C}
is modular then we can decompose
\mathcal{TM}
as follows:

\displaystyle\mathcal{TM}=\bigoplus_{I,J}\mathcal{TM}_{I}^{J}\vprod\epsilon_{I}^{J}.

We may then define the Frobenius structure in terms of this decomposition. This is the approach adopted by the following section.

6.
\mathcal{TM}
as a Frobenius Algebra

As before let
\mathcal{C}
be an MTC and let
\mathcal{M}
be a pivotal monoidal functor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{D}
where
\mathcal{D}
is a pivotal monoidal category. Before preceding with the description of a Frobenius algebra structure on
\mathcal{TM}
we give a brief outline of our strategy. Our first step is to equip
\mathcal{TM}
with the structure of an algebra. We do this by specifying a map

\displaystyle\nabla_{\textbf{X}}^{\textbf{Y},\textbf{Z}}\colon\Hom_{\mathcal{RTC}}(\textbf{X},\textbf{Y}\textbf{Z})

\displaystyle\to\Hom(\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{Y}}\otimes\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{Z}},\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{X}})

for all
\textbf{X},\textbf{Y},\textbf{Z}
in
\mathcal{RTC}
of the form
(AB,\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp}
. As
\mathcal{C}
is modular
\{(IJ,\epsilon_{I}^{J})^{\sharp}\}_{I,J\in\mathcal{I}}
forms a complete set of simples and
\nabla_{\textbf{X}}^{\textbf{Y},\textbf{Z}}
determines a map
\nabla\colon\mathcal{TM}\otimes\mathcal{TM}\to\mathcal{TM}
as described in Remark
A.2
. We then verify that this does indeed give an commutative algebra structure via Lemma
A.3
.

. This concludes the outline of the strategy.

Definition 6.1
.

Let
\textbf{X},\textbf{Y}
and
Z
be given by
(AB,\epsilon_{A}^{B})^{\sharp},(CD,\epsilon_{C}^{D})^{\sharp}
and
(EF,\epsilon_{E}^{F})^{\sharp}
respectively. Let
\alpha
be in
\Hom_{\mathcal{RTC}}(\textbf{X},\textbf{Y}\textbf{Z})=\Hom_{\mathcal{TC}}(\epsilon_{A}^{B},\epsilon_{C}^{D}\otimes_{\mathcal{TC}}\epsilon_{E}^{F})
. Recall from Proposition
3.4
that
\mathcal{TM}_{A}^{B}
is identified with the subspace of
\Hom_{D}(\mathcal{M}(AB),\tid)
characterised by (
3.4
). We consider the map

\displaystyle\Hom_{D}(\mathcal{M}(CD),\tid)\otimes\Hom_{D}(\mathcal{M}(EF),\tid)

\displaystyle\to\Hom_{D}(\mathcal{M}(AB),\tid)

\displaystyle f\otimes g

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathcal{TM}(\alpha)(f\otimes_{\mathcal{D}}g).

We note that the image of this map is in
\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{X}}=\mathcal{TM}_{A}^{B}
as

\displaystyle\mathcal{TM}(\epsilon_{A}^{B})\circ\mathcal{TM}(\alpha)(f\otimes_{\mathcal{D}}g)=\mathcal{TM}(\alpha\circ\epsilon_{A}^{B})(f\otimes_{\mathcal{D}}g)=\mathcal{TM}(\alpha)(f\otimes_{\mathcal{D}}g).

Therefore restricting this map to the subspace
\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{Y}}\otimes\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{Z}}
gives a map

\displaystyle\nabla_{\textbf{X}}^{\textbf{Y},\textbf{Z}}(\alpha)\colon\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{Y}}\otimes\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{Z}}\to\mathcal{TM}_{\textbf{X}}.

Let
\nabla:\mathcal{TM}\otimes\mathcal{TM}\to\mathcal{TM}
be the map constructed from
\nabla_{\textbf{X}}^{\textbf{Y},\textbf{Z}}(\alpha)
as described in Remark
A.2
.

Proposition 6.2
.

The morphisms
\nabla
and

\displaystyle u\vcentcolon=\id_{\tid_{\mathcal{D}}}\in\mathcal{TM}_{\tid}^{\tid}=\Hom_{\mathcal{RTC}}(\tidtc,\mathcal{TM})

form a product/unit pair that make
\mathcal{TM}
a
commutative
algebra.

The next step is to equip
\mathcal{TM}
with self-dualizing structure maps. For this to work we need to make some additional assumptions on
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
. Firstly we assume that the idempotent completion of
\mathcal{D}
, denoted
\overline{\mathcal{D}}
, is a multifusion category. Secondly we assume that
\overline{\mathcal{M}}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\overline{\mathcal{D}}
, obtained by composing
\mathcal{M}
with this embedding, is
indecomposable
. In other words, that there do not exist functors
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{1}
and
\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{2}
such that
\overline{\mathcal{M}}=\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1}\oplus\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2}
, where
\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{i}\leq\overline{\mathcal{D}}
.

,

Proposition 6.3
.

\overline{\mathcal{M}}
is indecomposable if and only if
\mathcal{TM}_{\tid}^{\tid}=\fld
. Furthermore, in this case, any non-zero
\alpha\in\mathcal{TM}_{X}^{Y}\leq\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M}(XY),\tid)
has a left-inverse in
\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\tid,\mathcal{M}(XY))
for all
X,Y
in
\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

By Proposition
3.4
,
\mathcal{TM}_{\tid}^{\tid}
is given by the subspace of
\End_{\mathcal{D}}(\tid)
such that

\displaystyle\alpha\otimes\id_{\mathcal{M}(Z)}=\id_{\mathcal{M}(Z)}\otimes\ \alpha\quad\forall Z\text{ in }\mathcal{C}.

Embedding this equality into
\overline{\mathcal{D}}
and decomposing gives

Therefore, if
\overline{\mathcal{M}}
is indecomposable,
\alpha_{i}=0
for any
i\in I
implies
\alpha=0
. This proves the second claim. ∎

A.4
. We therefore first establish the following perfect pairing.

by Proposition

. We now consider

(where

is given by (

)). Then the right-hand side of (
6.4
) is
\langle f,\tilde{g}\rangle
and so we are done. ∎

Remark 6.5
.

We note that this perfect pairing is
symmetric
with respect to the pivotal structure, i.e.
\langle f,g\rangle=\langle g,f\rangle
where
f\in\mathcal{TM}_{X}^{Y}=\mathcal{TM}_{X^{\vee\vee}}^{Y^{\vee\vee}}
.

Proposition 6.6
.

We consider
\mathcal{TM}
equipped with the algebra structure from Proposition
6.2
. We also equip
\mathcal{TM}
with the self-dualizing maps given by Lemma
6.4
and Lemma
A.4
with
c=d
(the dimension map for
\mathcal{RTC}

\mathcal{TM}
satisfies (
30
), i.e. is a Frobenius algebra.

3.4
and Lemma

Theorem 6.7
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an MTC and let
\mathcal{M}
be a pivotal tensor functor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{D}
such that
\overline{\mathcal{M}}
is indecomposable. Then
\mathcal{TM}
is a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra.

Proof.

This result follows from Proposition
6.3
, Proposition
6.2
, Proposition
6.6
and Remark
6.5
. ∎

Remark 6.8
.

The work of Buguieres and Natale
[
BN11
,
BN14
]
allows for an alternative perspective
\mathcal{TM}
and the algebraic structures it admits. They show that if a monoidal functor
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
admits a right adjoint
\mathcal{M}^{\text{ad}}\colon\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}
then
\mathcal{M}^{\text{ad}}(\tid_{\mathcal{D}})
admits a canonical half-braiding and product yielding a commutative algebra in
Z(\mathcal{C})

[
BN14
, Proposition 5.1]
. As we have supposed
\mathcal{C}
to be modular and therefore semisimple, the functor

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{\text{ad}}\colon\mathcal{D}

\displaystyle\to\mathcal{C}

\displaystyle A

\displaystyle\mapsto\bigoplus_{S}\Hom_{D}(\mathcal{M}(S),A)\cdot S

is right adjoint to
\mathcal{M}
and the resulting object
\mathcal{M}^{\text{ad}}(\tid_{\mathcal{D}})
in
Z(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{RTC}
coincides with
\mathcal{TM}
.

Combining Theorem
6.7
with the aforementioned
result of Kong and Runkel

[
KR09
, Theorem 3.4]
we obtain the following.

Corollary 6.9
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an MTC and let
\mathcal{M}
be a pivotal tensor functor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{D}
such that
\overline{\mathcal{M}}
is indecomposable and
\sum_{IJ}\dim(\mathcal{TM}_{I}^{J})d(I)d(J)=d(\mathcal{C})
. Then
Z(\mathcal{TM})
is a modular invariant.

Proof.

As
\sum_{IJ}\dim(\mathcal{TM}_{I}^{J})d(I)d(J)
is the dimension of
\mathcal{TM}
as an object in
\mathcal{RTC}\cong\CC
, the claim follows immediately from Theorem
6.7
and

[
KR09
, Theorem 3.4]
. ∎

7.
Module Categories and
\alpha
-induction

Definition 7.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a monoidal category. A
module category
over
\mathcal{C}
is a monoidal category
\mathcal{B}
together with a monoidal functor
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\End(\mathcal{B})
, where
\End(\mathcal{B})
is the category of endofunctors on
\mathcal{B}
. For the remainder of this article all module categories are assumed to be semisimple with finitely many simple objects.

From a physical point of view Cardy
[
Car89
]
showed that the algebraic data of an
annular partition function
in a boundary (rational) conformal field theory is given by a module category over the corresponding MTC. The process known as
\alpha
-induction is an operator algebra technique developed by Böckenhauer and Evans
[
BE98
]
that produces a
toroidal partition function
(as described in the introduction) from an annular partition function. The aim of this section is to apply the
\mathcal{TM}
construction in the case when
\mathcal{M}
is a module category. In particular, we shall show that in this case
\mathcal{TM}
may be related to
\alpha
-induction.

Ostrik
[
Ost03
, Section 5]
rephrased
\alpha
-induction using categorical language in the following way. Let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a module category over a pre-modular tensor category
\mathcal{C}
, where
\mathcal{D}
denotes
\End(\mathcal{B})
and
\mathcal{B}
is a semisimple category with finitely many simple objects. For
X,Y
in
\mathcal{C}
we consider the subspace

\displaystyle\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(X,Y)\leq\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M}(X),\mathcal{M}(Y))

defined by the condition that
\beta\in\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(X,Y)
satisfies, for all
Z
in
\mathcal{C}
,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(X)\otimes\mathcal{M}(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(Z)\otimes\mathcal{M}(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(Y)\otimes\mathcal{M}(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(Z)\otimes\mathcal{M}(Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta\otimes\id}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(\overline{\sigma}_{ZX})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\otimes\beta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(\sigma_{ZY})}
\circlearrowleft

(23)

where
\sigma
and
\overline{\sigma}
are the braiding on
\mathcal{C}
and its opposite respectively. The principal claim of
\alpha
-induction is then as follows. Under the assumption that the dimensions of all the objects in
\mathcal{C}
are positive, the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix whose entries are given by the dimension of
\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(I,J^{\vee})
commutes with the modular data of
\mathcal{C}
. Furthermore if
\mathcal{M}
is irreducible then this matrix is a
modular invariant
(see Definition
1.1
).

Remark 7.2
.

The claim found in
[
Ost03
]
is actually that the
\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}
-matrix whose entries are given by the dimension of
\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(I,J)
commutes with the modular data of
\mathcal{C}
. However as the modular data always commutes with the charge conjugation matrix these statements are equivalent.

In
[
Ost03
]
Ostrik also provides the following example to prove the necessity of the condition that the objects in
\mathcal{C}
have positive dimension.

Example 7.3
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be the fusion category of representations of
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
. A complete set of simples in
\mathcal{C}
is given by
\{\underline{0},\underline{1}\}
, where
\underline{0}
is the tensor unit and
\underline{1}\otimes\underline{1}=\underline{0}
. We may then equip
\mathcal{C}
with the pivotal structure
\delta_{\underline{1}}=-\id_{\underline{1}}
(so that
d(\underline{1})=-1
). One may also check that setting
\sigma_{\underline{1},\underline{1}}=\id_{\underline{0}}
defines a (degenerate) braiding on the category and we obtain a pre-modular tensor category. We then consider the module category

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}

\displaystyle\to\Vect

\displaystyle\underline{0}

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathbb{K}

\displaystyle\underline{1}

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathbb{K}.

As the braiding is given by the identity, we have
\sigma=\overline{\sigma}
and Equation (
23
) reduces to a tautology. Therefore
\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(\underline{0},\underline{1})=\fld
and the resulting dimension matrix fails to commute with the T-matrix

\mathcal{T}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\
0&-1\end{array}\right).

We start by remarking that Condition
23
makes sense even when
\mathcal{D}
is an arbitrary tensor category. Therefore to connect Ostrik’s formulation of
\alpha
-induction to
\mathcal{TM}
we have the following.

Theorem 7.4
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a pre-modular tensor category and let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a pivotal monoidal functor. Then
\Hom_{\mathcal{M}}^{\sigma}(X,Y^{\vee})\cong\mathcal{TM}_{X}^{Y}
.

Proof.

) is given by

The alternative characterisation of
\mathcal{TM}_{I}^{J}
given by Theorem
7.4
allows for the following generalization of Corollary
4.5
to the pre-modular case.

Theorem 7.5
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a pre-modular tensor category, let
\mathcal{D}
be a pivotal monoidal category and let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a pivotal monoidal functor. Then
\mathcal{TM}
is T-invariant.

Proof.

Let
I,J\in\Irr(\mathcal{C})
be such that
\mathcal{TM}_{I}^{J}\neq 0
. Then, by Theorem
7.4
, there exists a non-zero map
\beta\in\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M}(I),\mathcal{M}(J^{\vee}))

7.4
). We have

where
\mathcal{T}
denotes the T-matrix and to make certain string manipulations clearer, we have chosen to write
\beta
upside-down instead of writing
\beta^{\vee}
. Therefore
Z(\mathcal{TM})_{IJ}\neq 0
implies
\mathcal{T}_{II}=\mathcal{T}_{JJ}
. As
\mathcal{T}
is diagonal that is precisely the condition that
Z(F)
commutes with
\mathcal{T}
. ∎

Our goal is therefore to reinterpret a module category
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\End(\mathcal{B})
as a pivotal monoidal functor. Initially, this may seem improbable as
\End(\mathcal{B})
admits a canonical pivotal structure and, excluding pathological examples, modules categories fail to be pivotal. However, we can study many interesting examples if we only require that
\mathcal{M}

induce a pivotal structure on its full image
. Let
\mathcal{D}
be the full image of
\mathcal{M}
in
\End(\mathcal{B})
, i.e. objects in
\mathcal{D}
are of the form
\mathcal{M}(X)
for
X
in
\mathcal{C}
and

\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M}(X),\mathcal{M}(Y))=\Hom_{\End(\mathcal{B})}(\mathcal{M}(X),\mathcal{M}(Y)).

Clearly
\mathcal{D}
is a rigid monoidal category.
Furthermore, it comes with a natural candidate pivotal structure:
\mathcal{M}(\delta_{X})
, where
\delta_{X}\colon^{\vee}X\to X^{\vee}
gives the pivotal structure on
\mathcal{C}
. As
\mathcal{M}
is a functor,
\mathcal{M}(\delta_{X})
is natural with respect to morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
; however, to give a pivotal structure on
\mathcal{D}
it must be natural with respect
all
morphisms in
\mathcal{D}
. In other words the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(^{\vee}Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(^{\vee}X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(Y^{\vee})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(X^{\vee})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(\delta_{Y})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{\vee}\alpha}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{M}(\delta_{X})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{\vee}}
\circlearrowleft

(26)

must commute for all
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M}(X),\mathcal{M}(Y))
. When this is satisfied and
\mathcal{D}
is equipped with the resulting pivotal structure, the functor
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
is automatically pivotal. We may therefore construct
\mathcal{TM}
and Theorem
7.4
guarantees that
Z(\mathcal{TM})
will give the same matrix as
\alpha
-induction. Furthermore, the inclusion
\mathcal{D}\hookrightarrow\End(\mathcal{B})
fully embeds
\mathcal{D}
into a multifusion category. We therefore obtain the following corollary of Theorem
6.7
and Corollary
6.9
.

Corollary 7.6
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an MTC and let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\End(\mathcal{B})
be an indecomposable semisimple module category over
\mathcal{C}
with finitely many simple objects that induces a pivotal structure on its full image. Then
\mathcal{TM}
is a haploid, symmetric, commutative Frobenius algebra. In particular,
Z(\mathcal{TM})
is a modular invariant if and only
\sum_{IJ}\dim(\mathcal{TM}_{I}^{J})d(I)d(J)=d(\mathcal{C})
.

Remark 7.7
.

Ostrik’s Example
7.3
also shows that the condition that
\mathcal{M}
be pivotal is necessary for the results of Section
4
and Section
6
. Indeed, one may check that his example fails to induce a pivotal structure on its full image.

8.
A Case Study: The Temperley-Lieb Category

The goal of this section is to describe a class of interesting examples of module categories that induce a pivotal structure on their full images.

Let
\beta
be in
\mathbb{C}^{*}
. The Temperley-Lieb category
\text{TL}(\beta)
is a
\mathbb{C}
-linear category whose set of objects is given by
\{\underline{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
where
\underline{n}
may be thought of as a collection of
n
dots along an interval. The space
\Hom(\underline{m},\underline{n})
is the span of planar
(m,n)
-tangles modulo the relation
t\sqcup u-\beta t
where t is a planar
(m,n)
-tangle and
u
is the unknot. Composition is then given by tangle composition. For a more detailed description, see, for example,
[
GW02
]
.
\text{TL}(\beta)
is a monoidal category whose tensor product satisfies
\underline{n}\otimes\underline{m}=\underline{n+m}
. Furthermore,
\text{TL}(\beta)
is rigid and every object admits a canonical choice of self dualizing maps

denoted
\cre_{n}\colon\underline{0}\to\underline{n}\otimes\underline{n}
and
\ann_{n}\colon\underline{n}\otimes\underline{n}\to\underline{0}
respectively. In the case when
\beta=-[2]_{q}
for a primitive even root of unity
q
,
\text{TL}(\beta)
admits a unique tensor ideal
\mathcal{N}

[
GW02
]
. Quotienting
\text{TL}(\beta)
by
\mathcal{N}
and idempotent completing the result yields a spherical fusion category we denote
\mathcal{C}
. Using a skein relation we may define a non-degenerate braiding on
\mathcal{C}
giving us a modular tensor category
[
Tur16
, Theorem 7.5.3]
. Let
h
be the the smallest positive integer such that
q^{2h}=1
or equivalently
[h]_{q}=0
;
h
is called the
Coxeter number
of
\mathcal{C}
.
\mathcal{C}
turns out to be equivalent to the category of integrable highest weight modules of
A_{1}^{(1)}
at level
k=h-2
, denoted
\Rep_{k}A_{1}^{(1)}
(for this equivalence to be pivotal one must equip
\text{TL}(\beta)
with a ‘twisted’ pivotal structure, or alternatively, consider the so-called “disoriented” diagrammatic category presented in
[
CMW09
, p. 5]
; for further details on this issue see
[
ST09
]
). In particular, a complete set of simples in
\mathcal{C}
has size
h-1
.

Let
\mathcal{Q}
be a symmetric quiver with non-degenerate eigenvalue
\beta
(here non-degenerate signifies there exists an eigenvector
(x_{i})=x
with non-zero entries), let
A
be the basic algebra spanned by vertices in
\mathcal{Q}
and let
B
be the
A
-bimodule spanned by arrows in
\mathcal{Q}
. We can construct a module category over
\text{TL}(\beta)
as follows

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{M}\colon\text{TL}(\beta)&\to A,A\mbox{-}\text{Bimod}=\End(\Mod{A})\\
\mathcal{M}(\underline{n})&=B^{\otimes n}\\
\mathcal{M}(\ann_{1})_{ij}&=\left(\phi_{ij}\colon v\otimes w\mapsto x_{j}\langle v,w\rangle\right)\\
\mathcal{M}(\cre_{1})_{ij}&=\Big(\varphi_{ij}\colon 1\mapsto x_{i}^{-1}\sum_{b}b\otimes b^{*}\Big).\end{split}

(27)

As
\cre_{1}
and
\ann_{1}
tensor generate
\text{TL}(\beta)
this fully determines
\mathcal{M}
. One advantage of considering module categories of this form is that they induce a pivotal structure on the full image (cf. Section
7
). To prove this we first consider the following lemma.

Lemma 8.1
.

\phi^{n}
and
\varphi^{n}
denote the image of
\mathcal{M}(\ann_{n})
and
\mathcal{M}(\cre_{n})
respectively. For
i,j\in Q_{0}
and
n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}
we have the following

\displaystyle\phi_{ji}^{n}(w\otimes v)=\frac{x_{i}}{x_{j}}\ \phi_{ij}^{n}(v\otimes w)

(28)

and

\displaystyle\varphi_{ji}^{n}=\frac{x_{i}}{x_{j}}\ T_{ij}^{n}\circ\varphi_{ij}^{n}

17.71858pt{k}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{B^{\otimes n-1}}^{{\kern-25.18437pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 17.71858pt\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-20.12804pt{j}\kern 17.71858pt{k}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{B^{\otimes n-1}}^{{\kern-17.56667pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 12.20222pt\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-13.955pt{j}\kern 12.20222pt{k}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{B^{\otimes n-1}}^{{\kern-16.43451pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 11.07007pt\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-12.82285pt{j}\kern 11.07007pt{k}}}}
and compute,

\displaystyle\phi_{ij}^{n}(b\otimes v\otimes w\otimes b^{*})

\displaystyle=\phi_{kj}^{n-1}(v\otimes w)\phi_{ik}(b\otimes b^{*})

\displaystyle=x_{k}\phi_{kj}^{n-1}(v\otimes w).

We then also have

\displaystyle\phi_{ji}^{n}(w\otimes b^{*}\otimes b\otimes v)

\displaystyle=\phi_{jk}^{n-1}(w\otimes v)\phi_{ki}(b^{*}\otimes b)

\displaystyle=x_{i}\phi_{jk}^{n-1}(w\otimes v)

\displaystyle=\frac{x_{i}x_{k}}{xj}\phi_{kj}^{n-1}(v\otimes w)

\displaystyle=\frac{x_{i}}{xj}\phi_{ij}^{n}(b\otimes v\otimes w\otimes b^{*}).

Therefore (
28
) is proved. To prove (
29
) we proceed more directly,

\displaystyle\frac{x_{i}}{x_{j}}\ T_{ij}^{n}\circ\varphi_{ij}^{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{x_{i}}{x_{j}}\ T_{ij}^{n}\circ\Big(\sum\limits_{k}(\id_{\underline{n-1}}\otimes\ \varphi_{kj}\otimes\id_{\underline{n-1}})\circ\varphi^{n-1}_{ik}\Big)

\displaystyle=\frac{x_{i}}{x_{j}}\sum\limits_{k}(\id_{\underline{1}}\otimes\ (T^{n-1}_{ik}\circ\varphi^{n-1}_{ik})\otimes\id_{\underline{1}})\circ(T^{1}_{kj}\circ\varphi_{kj})

\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{k}(\id_{\underline{1}}\otimes\ \varphi^{n-1}_{ki}\otimes\id_{\underline{1}})\circ\varphi_{jk}

\displaystyle=\varphi^{n}_{ji}

as desired. ∎

.

Once again, let
\mathcal{Q}
be a symmetric quiver with non-degenerate eigenvalue
\beta

\mathcal{M}

\mathcal{C}

Theorem 8.3

(
[
EO04
]
, Theorem 3.12)
.

Indecomposable semisimple module categories over
\mathcal{C}
with finitely many simple objects are classified by the double Dynkin quivers of type A, D, E.

Corollary 8.4
.

Every semisimple module category over
\mathcal{C}
with finitely many simple objects induces a pivotal structure on its full image.

Proof.

This follows immediately from Theorem
8.3
and Proposition
8.2
. ∎

Remark 8.6
.

Let
\mathcal{M}
be a module category over
\mathcal{C}
arising from some quiver
\mathcal{Q}
via (
27
) and let
n
be in
\mathcal{N}
. Then
\mathcal{TM}(\underline{n})
is the space of
cycles
of length
n
in
\mathcal{Q}
.

We are now ready to exploit the
\mathcal{TM}
construction to explain a well known pattern in the classification of modular invariants over
\mathcal{C}
.

Theorem 8.7

(C.I.Z. classification
[
CIZ87
]
)
.

The complete list of modular invariants over
\mathcal{C}
is as follows. To aid legibility, we present these modular invariants as partition functions, cf. (
2
).

\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}_{h-1}=

\displaystyle\,\sum_{a=1}^{h-1}\,|\chi_{a}|^{2}\ ,\qquad\qquad\qquad

\displaystyle\forall h\geq 3

\displaystyle{\mathcal{D}}_{{h\over 2}+1}=

\displaystyle\,\sum_{a=1}^{h-1}\,\chi_{a}\,\chi_{J^{a-1}a}^{*}\ ,\qquad\qquad\qquad

\displaystyle\text{ whenever}\ {h\over 2}\ \text{ is even}

\displaystyle{\mathcal{D}}_{{h\over 2}+1}=

\displaystyle\,|\chi_{1}+\chi_{J1}|^{2}+|\chi_{3}+\chi_{J3}|^{2}+\cdots+2|\chi_{{h\over 2}}|^{2}\ ,\qquad

\displaystyle\text{ whenever}\ {h\over 2}\ \text{ is\ odd}

\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{6}=

\displaystyle\,|\chi_{1}+\chi_{7}|^{2}+|\chi_{4}+\chi_{8}|^{2}+|\chi_{5}+\chi_{11}|^{2}\ ,\qquad\qquad

\displaystyle\text{ for}\ h=12

\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{7}=

\displaystyle\,|\chi_{1}+\chi_{17}|^{2}+|\chi_{5}+\chi_{13}|^{2}+|\chi_{7}+\chi_{11}|^{2}

\displaystyle\,+\chi_{9}\,(\chi_{3}+\chi_{15})^{*}+(\chi_{3}+\chi_{15})\,\chi^{*}_{9}+|\chi_{9}|^{2}\ ,\qquad\qquad

\displaystyle\text{ for}\ h=18

\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{8}=

\displaystyle\,|\chi_{1}+\chi_{11}+\chi_{19}+\chi_{29}|^{2}+|\chi_{7}+\chi_{13}+\chi_{17}+\chi_{23}|^{2}\ ,\qquad

\displaystyle\text{ for}\ h=30.

where
h
is the Coxeter number of
\mathcal{C}
and
J:\{1,2,...,h-1\}\to\{1,2,...,h-1\}
maps
a
to
h-a
.

As alluded to in the introduction, the classification of modular invariants over
\mathcal{C}
admits the following A-D-E pattern. Let
\mathcal{X}
be a double Dynkin quiver of type A,D or E. The eigenvalues of
\mathcal{X}
form a subset of
\{-[2]_{q}\mid q=e^{\frac{\pi il}{h}},1\leq l\leq h-1\}
for some
h\in\mathbb{N}
. Then, for
l\in\{1,2,\dots h-1\}
, the
l
th diagonal entry in the modular invariant associated to
\mathcal{X}
gives the dimension of the corresponding eigenspace of
\mathcal{X}
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be an A-D-E double Dynkin quiver and let
\mathcal{M}\colon\mathcal{C}\to A,A\mbox{-}\text{Bimod}
be the corresponding module category over
\mathcal{C}
. It is known that applying
\alpha
-induction, as described in Section
7
, to
\mathcal{M}
yields the modular invariant associated to
\mathcal{X}
by the list appearing in Theorem
8.7

[
BE01
, Section 5]
. However, even once this connection has been established it is non-trivial to explain the A-D-E pattern described above. The
\mathcal{TM}
construction explains this pattern in the following way. Let
Z
be the modular invariant obtained by applying
\alpha
-induction to
\mathcal{M}
. By Theorem
7.4
the entries of
Z
may be thought of as the dimensions of the simple multiplicity spaces in
\mathcal{TM}
, in other words

\displaystyle Z=Z(\mathcal{TM})

where
Z(\mathcal{TM})
is given by Definition
3.6
.

We recall that
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid)
is a semisimple commutative algebra generated by the orthogonal primitive idempotents
\{\tid_{I}\}_{I\in\mathcal{I}}
where
(\tid,\tid_{I})^{\sharp}=(II^{\vee},e_{I}^{I\vee})^{\sharp}
, see Remark
2.8
.
The diagonal terms in
Z
therefore correspond to the dimensions of the weight spaces of the action of
\End_{\mathcal{TC}}(\tid)=\mathcal{K}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{C})
on
TM(\tid)
. However by Proposition
8.5
this action coincides with the natural action of
\mathcal{K}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{C})
on
\mathcal{K}_{\mathbb{C}}(\Mod\!\mbox{-}A)
. As the weight spaces of this action are given by the eigenspaces of
\mathcal{X}
this explains the pattern.

Appendix A
Lemmas on Frobenius Algebras

The purpose of this section is to provide the necessary definitions on Frobenius algebras followed by certain technical results required in Section
6
.

We also use

to denote the
unit
and

to denote the
counit
.
A
is called
haploid
if is satisfies
\Hom_{\mathcal{B}}(\tid,A)=\mathbb{C}
. If
\mathcal{B}
is braided then
A
is called

Lemma A.3
.

Let
A
be an object in
\mathcal{B}
and let
\nabla
be in
\Hom_{\mathcal{B}}(A\otimes A,A)
. Then
\nabla
is associative if

\displaystyle\nabla^{RS,T}_{RST}(\id)\big(\nabla^{R,S}_{RS}(\id)(f\otimes g)\otimes h\big)=\nabla^{R,ST}_{RST}(\id)\big(f\otimes\nabla^{S,T}_{ST}(\id)(g\otimes h)\big)

(37)

for all
R,S,T\in\Irr(\mathcal{B})
,
\alpha\in\Hom_{\mathcal{B}}(R,ST)
,
f\in A_{R}
,
g\in A_{S}
and
h\in A_{T}
. An element
u\in A_{\tid}
is a unit for
\nabla
if

\displaystyle\nabla^{\tid,S}_{S}(\id)(u\otimes g)=g\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla^{S,\tid}_{S}(\id)(g\otimes u)=g

(38)

Furthermore, if
\mathcal{B}
is braided then

is commutative if
